name: Dejima
label: Dejima
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/484294967: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dejima Dutch Trading Post' (254 m across).
notes: Former Dutch trading post on a fan-shaped island.

text.description:
Dejima was a small artificial island built in Nagasaki in 1636 to hold foreign traders. For 220 years it was Japan's main channel for trade and cultural exchange with the West, and the Dutch were based here from 1641 until 1858. The island measured only about 120 m by 75 m and was joined to the mainland by one small bridge. Land reclamation later folded it into the city, so today you are looking at a historic site within Nagasaki rather than a true island. It was named a national historic site in 1922, and work continues to bring back its island setting.

It suits a phone because the story is told by the setting: a compact, enclosed site with a clear sense of place. Stay back from the middle and take a wide view first, then move in for details such as rooflines, doorways, signs and any flags. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m east of the subject. From here you can take a wide first view of the site. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines on, and tap on the building you want so the exposure is set for it, not for the sky. Access to parts of the site may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Dejima is in Nagasaki, Japan, on the site of the former artificial island that is now part of the city after land reclamation.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Dejima (出島) in central Nagasaki using a map app. Check the official site for the current entrance arrangements. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall scene. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move closer and want to fit in more of the site. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as roof edges, windows and signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From here you can take in a wide view of the site before you walk in closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level. Frame the whole site with the default lens (1x), then take a second shot with a doorway, wall or other foreground element in the edge of the frame for depth. Finish with a tighter telephoto shot of one detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so pale walls don't wash out. Use portrait mode only for a person standing in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good choice, as the sun is in the east behind you when you face west from where you stand. Overcast days also work, because the light is even and the walls show no harsh shadows.

text.access_note: Parts of the site may be ticketed or have set visiting times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum
label: Atomic Bomb Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.

notes: Museum telling the story of the bombing of Nagasaki.

text.description:
The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum is a place of remembrance for the atomic bombing of the city on 9 August 1945, at 11:02 in the morning. It was completed in April 1996 and replaced the older International Culture Hall, where relics from the bombing had first been shown. It stands in Nagasaki Peace Park, beside the Nagasaki National Peace Memorial Hall for the Atomic Bomb Victims, which was built in 2003. Inside, the story runs from the city before the bomb through the aftermath and rebuilding to today's calls for peace. One of the objects on show is a clock stopped at 11:02.

As a photograph, the museum works best as a quiet, respectful record of the place rather than a showy picture. The building and its neighbour make a calm, well-ordered scene, and the surrounding park gives you room to step back and fit the walls into the frame. Keep people in the shot to a minimum and avoid anything that feels staged. This is a site of mourning for many visitors.

For your phone, use the exterior of the building and the park around it. Photography rules inside are not covered here, so check the official site before you go and follow any signs once you are in the galleries.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Nagasaki, in Nagasaki Peace Park, next to the Nagasaki National Peace Memorial Hall for the Atomic Bomb Victims.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Navigate to the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum (長崎原爆資料館) in Nagasaki Peace Park. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so there is no further walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building as you see it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the whole front in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the entrance or the lines of the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. To photograph it, walk out into the surrounding park and turn back to face the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so the walls look straight. Hold the phone level, and include a little open ground or sky to give a sense of calm. For a second picture, move sideways so the neighbouring Peace Memorial Hall appears alongside, which shows how the two buildings sit together. Keep strangers out of the frame, or let them be small and unidentifiable.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Skip portrait mode and heavy filters; a plain, natural image suits the subject better.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight with soft or evenly overcast light tends to give the cleanest, least glaring pictures of the building. Earlier or quieter parts of the day usually mean fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The museum is a place of remembrance, so check the official site before you go for entry details and the rules on photography inside.

name: Nagasaki Peace Park
label: Peace Park
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/497061000: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nagasaki Peace Park' (377 m across).
notes: Memorial park for the victims of the 1945 atomic bombing.

text.description: Nagasaki Peace Park was opened in 1955 to remember the atomic bombing of the city on 9 August 1945. It is a long, calm stretch of paths, trees and sculpture, next to the Atomic Bomb Museum and near the Peace Memorial Hall. It photographs well because the key subjects are spread out along one line. At the south end is the Fountain of Peace, built in 1969. At the north end stands the 10-metre Peace Statue by Nagasaki sculptor Seibo Kitamura, with the right hand pointing to the threat of nuclear weapons and the extended left hand symbolising eternal peace. Between them are the monuments of the Peace Symbols Zone, begun in 1978, where countries and sister cities gave sculptures. One example is the 260 cm bronze 'Joy of Life', a mother lifting her baby. Close to the hypocenter you can also see part of a concrete wall from Urakami Cathedral. A black stone monolith marks the spot beneath where the bomb exploded, 500 metres up, at 11:02 that morning. This is a place of remembrance, so keep your phone use quiet and unhurried, and avoid posing in a way that would feel out of place. Use the path as a leading line, wait for a gap in the people, and let the statue or a sculpture fill the frame. Details such as the fountain plaque and the monolith make good close-ups.
text.geographic_location: Nagasaki Peace Park is in Nagasaki, Japan, right next to the Atomic Bomb Museum and close to the Peace Memorial Hall. It is built around the hypocenter of the 1945 explosion.
text.directions_text: It is about 216 m south of the middle of the park. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the long view up the park. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and sculpture in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the faces of statues, plaques and the Peace Statue from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Walk a little further in for closer shots of individual sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the main path on a line so it leads the eye into the park. Keep the horizon level, and put a statue or the fountain on one third with trees or sky beside it. For the Peace Statue, step back, hold the phone vertically to include its full height, then zoom in for a close detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the subject to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so bright sky or pale stone does not wash out. Portrait mode can work on the smaller sculptures, but check that the edges look natural.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Expect a much busier, more formal atmosphere around 9 August, the day of the annual ceremony.

text.access_note: This is a public park and memorial; there may be restrictions around events and ceremonies, so check the official site before you go.

name: Glover Garden
label: Glover Garden
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/552140518: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Glover Garden' (359 m across).
notes: Hillside park with western-style merchant houses and harbour views.

text.description: Glover Garden is a hillside park above Nagasaki harbour, built around the home of Thomas Blake Glover, a Scottish merchant who played a part in modernising Japan's shipbuilding, coal mining and other industries. The Glover Residence, completed in 1863, is the oldest surviving Western-style house in Japan. It was built by a Japanese carpenter, Hidenoshin Koyama, so the frame is Japanese while the stone-floored verandas, latticed arches and French windows are foreign touches. Look up for the tile roof with its demon-headed tiles and the British-style chimneys added later. The house is also nicknamed the "Madame Butterfly House", and statues of Puccini and the singer Miura Tamaki stand nearby. The park also holds Ringer House (1865) and Alt House, plus the preserved stone gate of the old Nagasaki Masonic Lodge, so there are plenty of small subjects as well as the big view. It photographs well because the old buildings, gardens and harbour outlook sit close together. Use the verandas and garden paths as natural frames. The park is open to the public and gets nearly two million visitors a year, so expect people in your shots at busy times. Take wide pictures first, then move closer for the roof tiles, chimneys and window details.
text.geographic_location: Glover Garden is on the Minamiyamate hillside in Nagasaki, looking out over the harbour. It is a large park of several historic Western-style houses, about 360 metres across.
text.directions_text: No tram stop or station was listed for this spot, so navigate to Glover Garden on the Minamiyamate hillside above Nagasaki harbour. Once you are at the phone icon on the map, the middle of the garden is about 1 minute on foot to the south. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole garden and the harbour beyond. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the houses and paths. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the demon-headed roof tiles, chimneys and statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Walk a few steps along the path for a cleaner angle if other visitors are in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, especially if the harbour is in the background. Use a veranda arch, tree branches or a garden path as a frame around the house. Take one wide shot, one at the default lens (1x), then a close detail shot such as roof tiles or a window.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the house to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the white walls and roof tiles keep their detail. Try portrait mode for a person standing in front of the statues or a veranda.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the day usually gives softer light and fewer people. Check the official site for opening times before you go.

text.access_note: Glover Garden is a visitor attraction that is open to the public, but entry arrangements may apply, so check the official site before you go.

name: Urakami Cathedral
label: Urakami Cathedral
camera_source: Commons cluster (4 photos), weak. Moved 35 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 530 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/280652259: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Urakami Cathedral' (84 m across).
notes: Rebuilt Catholic cathedral near the atomic bomb hypocenter.

text.description: Urakami Cathedral, also called the Immaculate Conception Cathedral, is the Catholic cathedral of Nagasaki, and its twin-towered brick-coloured front makes a strong, simple subject for a phone photo. The story behind it is part of why people stop here. Local Christians, whose faith had been banned and who were sent into exile between 1869 and 1873, began building the first cathedral in 1895 on land where they had once been forced to tread on sacred images. When it was finished in 1925 it was the largest Christian building in the Asia-Pacific region. The atomic bomb of 9 August 1945 exploded only about 500 m away and destroyed it. The congregation rebuilt on the same site, finishing in October 1959, and in 1980 the walls were re-faced with brick tiles to look more like the original. Today a bell and the damaged statue known as the Atom-bombed Mary are displayed in the grounds, so there is more to see and photograph once you are close. For photographs, the front with its two towers is the natural frame. It is a working place of worship and a memorial, so keep your photography quiet and unobtrusive, and avoid pointing your phone at people who are praying.
text.geographic_location: In the Motoomachi area of Nagasaki, in the Urakami district. The Nagasaki Peace Park is nearby.
text.directions_text: No tram stop or station was available for this spot. Head for the Urakami and Motoomachi area of Nagasaki and ask for Urakami Cathedral. Walk north-east from it to reach the cathedral grounds. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From where you stand, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the cathedral closer. Switch to the default lens (1x) as you get nearer, and use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you can stand close to the front and want both towers and the entrance in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 平和公園 (Nagasaki Peace Park) (beyond the Peace Statue, on the far side of the park). A distance view of the rebuilt cathedral standing on its hill, with the surrounding neighbourhood below it. At that distance the building will be small at 1x, so zoom in or walk closer to the grounds for a bigger picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the twin towers and turn on gridlines so the verticals stay straight. Hold the phone level, because tilting it up makes the towers lean inwards. Once you are in the grounds, a second photo of the bell or the Atom-bombed Mary can add context to the story of the place.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral front to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright and the brickwork is turning dark. A sharper, steadier shot comes from holding the phone with both hands and resting your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters brick-coloured walls and avoids harsh midday shadows. Early in the day there are also likely to be fewer people in your frame.

text.access_note: This is a working cathedral and memorial site, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any rules about photography or dress.

name: Suwa Shrine
label: Suwa Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '大門' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/544258615: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Suwa-jinja' (163 m across).
notes: Large hillside shrine reached by a long stone stairway.

text.description:
Suwa Shrine is the main Shinto shrine of Nagasaki, set on the slopes of Mount Tamazono in the northern part of the city. You climb a long stone staircase to reach it, and the effort pays off at the gate, 大門, which people often call the face of the shrine. Looking back out from the gate, you see the vermilion approach in front of you and the city and its residential rooftops spread out below the hill.

The shrine's official founding date is 1614, and the main building was completed in 1626. It came through the atomic bombing of 9 August 1945 still standing, which locals noted at the time. Each year on 7 to 9 October it hosts the Nagasaki Kunchi, one of Japan's major festivals.

For photos, the gate works as a natural frame: red woodwork around the edges, the city beyond. Take your time on the climb, as the stairs are often given as 277 steps, though counts vary. Pause on the way up for a few shots of the stone approach and lanterns. If you have the energy, the large stone-lantern-lined torii at the lower end and the tunnel of small vermilion torii at the Tamazono Inari shrine are both worth a few frames. This is a working place of worship, so keep your voice down and don't block the path while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Suwa Shrine is in the northern part of Nagasaki, on the slopes of Mount Tamazono above the city. It is reached by a long stone staircase up the hillside.
text.directions_text: The streetcar stop Suwa Jinja is a few minutes' walk from the shrine; from there you climb the stone staircase to the gate. There is parking for visitors at the top. Allow extra time for the steps and for photo stops on the way up. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and the view through it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the approach and the city in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops and details below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on 大門, inside the gate, facing out over the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the gate's edges parallel to the lines so the frame looks straight. Place the horizon on the upper third and let the red approach lead the eye down to the city. For a different shot, try the large torii flanked by big stone lanterns (一の鳥居) on your way up, or the tunnel of vermilion torii at 玉園稲荷神社.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or city to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit scene doesn't wash out. After dusk, use night mode and hold the phone against the gate post or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening or after dusk, when the stone steps are lit and the city lights come on. Check opening arrangements first, as the long torii walkway may close after normal visiting hours.

text.access_note: This is an active Shinto shrine, so dress and behave respectfully, and check the official site before you go, especially for evening visits.

name: Sōfuku-ji
label: Sofuku-ji
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3927261657: the OpenStreetMap point 'Soufukuji Temple'.
notes: Chinese-style Obaku Zen temple with a vermilion gate.

text.description: Sōfuku-ji is a Chinese-style Zen temple in Nagasaki, founded in 1629 by the Chinese monk Chaoran as the family temple for people from Fuzhou who had settled in the city. It photographs well because it looks quite different from most Japanese temples. The bright red Ryugamon, or 'Gate of the Dragon Palace', is a rare example of South Chinese Ming-style architecture. The current gate dates from 1849, after earlier versions were lost to fires and storms. Further in, the Daiyū Hōden Buddha Hall is one of Nagasaki's oldest buildings. Its sections were cut in China, shipped over and assembled here in 1646. Two of its buildings are designated national treasures. Together the buildings give you strong colour, carved timber and layered rooflines in a small area. Look too for the large cauldron made by the priest Qianhai to cook gruel during the famine of 1681, and for the Masodo, which enshrines Maso, the Chinese goddess of the sea. Start with one wide shot of the red gate to set the scene. Then move closer for details such as roof ends, painted beams and lanterns. The grounds are fairly compact, so you can cover the main views in a short visit. Be considerate of people praying or visiting, and keep out of the way of doorways and paths.
text.geographic_location: Sōfuku-ji is in the city of Nagasaki, Japan.
text.directions_text: A tram stop named after the temple is reported nearby; check current routes locally. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

Put the red gate in the centre or on a third, and let the roof line sit near the top of the frame. Hold your phone level and avoid tilting up too much, which makes buildings lean. For details, zoom in on roof ends, beams and lanterns, and leave some space around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red paintwork to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the red stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Under covered halls, night mode may help if it is dim, but hold the phone steady for a couple of seconds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the red paint and carved timber, and fewer harsh shadows. The temple is listed as open daily from 8am to 5pm, but check the official site before you go.

name: Oura Church
label: Oura Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).

notes: Oldest surviving wooden Gothic church in Japan.

text.description: Oura Church is a white Gothic basilica, and its single octagonal tower and pale walls make a clean, recognisable subject for a phone photo. A small wooden church was finished here in 1864, built for the French community and named after the Twenty-Six Martyrs of Japan. The larger church you see now dates from around 1878. It is made of white stuccoed brick, has five aisles, and its stained glass was brought from France. The church is also tied to a well-known moment in Japanese Christian history. In March 1865 a group of villagers from nearby Urakami came to the doors and quietly told the priest that they shared his faith. They were descendants of Christians who had gone into hiding more than two centuries earlier. A bronze relief in the courtyard shows the scene. The building was named a National Treasure in 1933, its grounds became a National Historic Site in 2012, and it joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018 with eleven other related sites. For photos, the white façade and steep roofline suit a straight-on view with the tower on one side of the frame. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m north-east of the subject. That makes it easy to include the whole building and a little of its surroundings. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, then walk closer for details such as the windows and the bronze relief.
text.geographic_location: Oura Church stands in the Ōura area of Nagasaki, on Kyushu.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so start from central Nagasaki and go by taxi or hired scooter to the Ōura area. Head south-west and keep the church's tower in view. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole church with some of its surroundings. Switch to 2x or 3x telephoto, if your phone has it, to pick out the tower and façade from this distance. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only once you are close, as it makes the building look narrow at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. This gives a view of the whole building from a distance. Then walk the short way down for closer shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the tower on one of the vertical lines so it stands straight. Keep the whole roofline in the frame with a little space above it. Up close, step back a few paces and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the façade, or use 2x for the stained glass and the courtyard relief.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls keep their detail and don't turn pale. If the sky is bright, check that the tower hasn't lost its shape.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer on the white walls and there are usually fewer people in the courtyard. Check the church's opening times before planning your visit.

text.access_note: Oura Church is a working Catholic church and a heritage site that may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mount Inasa
label: Mount Inasa
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4641487651: the OpenStreetMap point '稲佐山'.
notes: Observation deck with the famous night view of Nagasaki.

text.description:
Mount Inasa is the hill on the west side of Nagasaki, and its summit is the classic place to look back over the whole city. The hill rises to 333 metres, and from the top you see the harbour, the streets climbing the opposite slopes and the mountains beyond. A multi-level observation deck near the summit has a rooftop with a 360-degree panoramic view, so you can turn all the way round and shoot in every direction without moving far.

It is best known for its night view. Nagasaki's night view was named one of the "World's New Three Great Night Views" in 2021, and the outlook from Mount Inasa is called the "10 Million Dollar Night View". That reputation makes it a good place to stay on for the evening if your phone has a night mode.

For photos, use the upper levels of the deck for the widest, clearest view, and the lower levels when you want a different angle on the city. Come for the daytime light and stay on if you can, as the scene changes a lot as the lights come on. Glass and railings can cause reflections, so hold the phone close to the glass, or shoot over the rail where that is allowed. Inasayama Park, with its playground, outdoor stage and lawn seating, is also on the mountain.
text.geographic_location: Mount Inasa is a hill in the west of Nagasaki, rising above the city and the harbour. The observation deck is a short walk from the top stations of the ropeway and the slope car.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so start from central Nagasaki and head west towards the hill. The Nagasaki Ropeway and the Nagasaki Inasa Mountain Slope Car both run to the summit, and their top stations sit next to each other. From there it is a short walk to the observation deck. Check the official sites for the ropeway and slope car before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main city view, then switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the rooftop to take in more of the 360-degree scene. Use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out details such as the harbour or single hillsides.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is right there, so the photo is the view you get from the top. Turn around on the observation deck to choose your direction.

name: Megane Bridge
label: Megane Bridge
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5336401732: the OpenStreetMap point 'Megane Bridge'.
notes: Stone double-arch bridge whose reflection looks like a pair of glasses.

text.description: Megane Bridge is a small stone bridge over the Nakashima River in Nagasaki. Its name means Spectacles Bridge: it has two arches, and when the water is calm each arch is mirrored below it, so the pair of round shapes looks like a pair of glasses. That reflection is the photo to go for. The bridge was built in 1634 by Mokusu Nyojo, a Chinese monk who lived at Kofukuji Temple. It is said to be one of the oldest stone arch bridges in Japan, and it is an Important Cultural Property. It has been rebuilt before: a flood destroyed it in 1647 and it was rebuilt the next year. A severe flood in July 1982 damaged it badly, but nearly all the original stones were recovered and it was put back as it was. Only pedestrians may cross, so you can usually stand and compose a picture without traffic in the way. Look closely at the stonework along the embankment for the small heart-shaped stones, around twenty of them. They make a charming close-up detail. Frame the full double arch with its reflection first, then move in for the stones. Keep your phone steady against the railing or your body, and check the screen for tilted lines, because a leaning bridge is the most common problem here.
text.geographic_location: Megane Bridge crosses the Nakashima River in Nagasaki, and is one of the group of stone bridges built along this river.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; use a map app to reach the Megane Bridge area on the Nakashima River. From there, the bridge is about 71 m to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in both arches and their reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you have to stand very close, and keep the bridge away from the edges of the frame so it doesn't stretch. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the heart-shaped stones and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From here you can see the whole bridge and its reflection in one frame. Then walk towards it for closer shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the water's surface up with a horizontal grid line, so the arches and their reflection sit level and symmetrical. Leave a little water in the foreground so the reflected circles are complete. Then take a close shot of the embankment stones to find the hearts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arches to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky doesn't wash out the stonework. Take a few shots in case ripples spoil one. A Live Photo can help you pick the moment the water is stillest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the water is calm, as that gives the clearest reflection. Early morning or late afternoon is often gentler for stone and water than harsh midday sun.

text.description:
Nagasaki Shinchi Chinatown is a shopping strip that runs across several blocks of central Nagasaki, with Chinese-style shopfronts, food stalls and decorations along the streets. It photographs well because it is compact and busy with colour, so you can shoot wide street scenes and close details within a few minutes' walk. The area is about 253 m across, so it is easy to cover on foot.

The history gives your photos some context. The land was once used for the warehouses of Chinese merchants, who traded goods to Japan between the 15th and 19th centuries. Nagasaki was the only port the Tokugawa government left open to Chinese and Dutch traders, and the Chinese traders lived in the 'Chinese residence' (Tojin yashiki) a little to the south-east, in today's Kannaimachi. Most of today's Chinese community here is of Fuzhounese descent, and Nagasaki became a sister city of Fuzhou in 1980.

Then wander into the streets for close-ups of signs, lanterns and food. Keep a little space around shopfronts and stalls, and ask before you photograph people at close range.

From it, the middle of Chinatown is 73 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 75 m south-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright sign or lantern to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich instead of washed out. After dark, let Night mode run and hold the phone still against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening is a good choice, because shop lighting and any lanterns show up well as the daylight fades. Mornings are likely to be quieter if you want clearer street views.

text.description:
The Peace Statue is a memorial figure in Nagasaki, and it is one of the places people come to photograph as a reminder of the city's history. It is a large, simple subject, so it works well on a phone. The shape stands out cleanly against the sky, and you do not need any special settings to get a good picture.

The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south-west of the subject. That is close enough to take a clear photo without much walking, and far enough back to fit the whole figure in the frame. Looking north-east from there, you can show the statue with some space around it, which helps it feel calm and dignified rather than crowded in.

This is a place of remembrance, so take your time. Keep your voice down, don't pose in a way that would feel disrespectful, and be patient if other visitors are standing in front of the statue. A short wait usually gives you a clear view. Try one wide photo that shows the statue in its surroundings, then a closer one of the figure alone. Check the result on your screen and retake it if the sky looks too bright or the statue too dark.

text.directions_text: Once you arrive, the statue is about 23 metres north-east of it, a short walk. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

name: Sannō Shrine
label: Sanno Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '一本柱鳥居' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6380332923: the OpenStreetMap point 'Sanno Shrine'.
notes: Known for its one-legged torii gate that survived the atomic blast.

text.description:
Sannō Shrine is a shrine in Nagasaki, and its best-known sight is the one-legged stone torii (一本柱鳥居) at the entrance. The gate was damaged by the atomic bomb blast on 9 August 1945. One pillar was knocked down, but the other stayed upright, so the gate now stands as a single column with its upper beam still above it. The shockwave also turned the torii about 30 degrees on its base. The shrine is roughly 800 metres from the hypocentre. It is a place of remembrance, so take your photos calmly and quietly.

The torii photographs well because of its shape. Seen from the approach path at the top of the stone steps, the surviving pillar and beam stand out against the sky as a simple, strong silhouette, and this is the view most often recommended. Keep the whole gate in the frame so that the missing half is clear to the viewer. The shrine also has two large camphor trees. The bomb scorched them and stripped their leaves, yet they survived, and new growth has covered the dead wood. They make a good second photo, with the trunk and its healed, layered bark filling the frame. Leave room for other visitors and avoid blocking the steps or the path.
text.geographic_location: Sannō Shrine is in Nagasaki, about 800 metres south-east of the atomic bomb hypocentre. The torii stands at the shrine entrance.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so start from the atomic bomb hypocentre area. The shrine is about 800 metres south-east of the hypocentre, a short walk. The torii is at the top of the stone steps leading up to the shrine. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the torii looks natural. If you can't step back far enough to fit the whole gate in, try the ultra-wide (0.5x). Keep the phone upright so the single pillar looks tall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can see the single-pillar torii against the sky, with the surviving pillar and the upper beam fully in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the pillar on one of the vertical lines, with plenty of sky around the beam. Crouch a little and tilt the phone up slightly so that the silhouette stays clean, but check that the pillar still looks straight. Take one wide shot to show the whole gate, then a closer one with the telephoto (2x) of the beam and pillar.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the torii to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone becomes a clear silhouette. Keep the phone steady, or brace your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is easiest because the sky behind the torii is clear. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer visitors.

text.access_note: The shrine appears to be an open place of worship, but check the official site before you go and be respectful of the grounds.

Its collection covers art connected with Nagasaki, along with a group of Spanish works gathered by Suma Yakichiro, who was a special envoy to Spain during the Second World War. The museum opened in the same year as the Nagasaki Museum of History and Culture. Together they replaced the older Nagasaki Prefectural Museum and Art Museum, which closed at the end of 2002.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the building itself. Look for lines, shapes and edges in the building; these work well with gridlines switched on. Then move closer and look for details such as corners, glass, railings and reflections.

Keep the phone level so vertical edges stay straight. Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Walk around a little before you settle on a view, and leave people in the frame if you want a sense of scale. Rules on photography inside galleries can differ from room to room, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: This is the memorial to the 26 Christians who were put to death on Nishizaka Hill on 5 February 1597. Twenty were Japanese and six were foreign priests. They had been arrested in Kyoto and Osaka and made to walk to Nagasaki. The monument and the museum were built in June 1962 to mark 100 years since the martyrs were canonised. The wide bronze relief of the figures is by the Japanese sculptor Yasutake Funakoshi, who spent four years on it. It photographs well because the open square in front of it sits at the top of the hill, so you can fit the bronze and the town's rooftops into one picture. Beside the monument is St Philip's Church, built for the same anniversary and designed in the style of Gaudí. Its shapes make a good second subject. Pope John Paul II visited in 1981 and Pope Francis in 2019. The place is a memorial, so keep voices low and avoid posing in a way that blocks others who have come to pay their respects. Take one wide shot to show the monument with the city behind it, then step closer for a tighter frame of the figures. Look for small details too, such as the faces, hands and the texture of the bronze. If you want a cityscape, turn around and use the monument as a dark foreground shape.
text.geographic_location: On Nishizaka Hill in Nagasaki, in the park grounds beside the Twenty-Six Martyrs Museum and St Philip's Church. The hill rises steeply above the area around Nagasaki Station.
text.directions_text: From Nagasaki Station, the monument is about a ten-minute walk, and the last stretch climbs a steep hill. Once at the top, walk into the open square in front of the monument. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole bronze monument and the rooftops behind it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the figures' faces and details.

Keep your phone level so the monument's vertical lines stay straight, and hold it a little low rather than tilting it upwards. For a second view, turn around to the city side and use part of the monument at the edge of the frame as a foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the metal keeps its detail. Hold the phone with both hands, because the ultra-wide lens makes small shakes more visible in low light.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the bronze, and the square is often quieter then.

text.description:
Kōshi-byō is the Confucian shrine built by Nagasaki's Chinese community, and it gives you a very different set of photos from the rest of the city. The buildings are Chinese in style, with strong shapes and bold colour. Outside the shrine stand 72 statues, one for each of the 72 followers of Confucius. They make good foreground subjects for a phone photo.

Some history helps you choose your shots. The shrine was first built in 1893 by Chinese residents of Nagasaki, with support from the Qing dynasty government, as a place of worship and learning. It was badly damaged by the atomic bomb on 9 August 1945. It reopened to the public in September 1967 and was renovated extensively in 1982. The land is now owned by the Chinese Embassy in Tokyo. A building at the rear houses a museum of Chinese history, with large illuminated photographs of the old Silk Road and loaned treasures from Beijing.

For photos, work from the outside in. Start with a wide view of the main building, then move closer for the statues and the roof and doorway details. The statues work well in a row, so line them up and let them lead the eye towards the shrine. If other visitors are in the way, wait a moment or shoot a tighter detail instead. Check which parts you may photograph, especially inside the museum, on the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Confucius Shrine is in Nagasaki.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the Gimon gate, the yellow-tiled front gate). The shrine's front gate with its yellow tiled roof and dragon roof ornaments, framed by the entrance grounds. Walk closer for statue shots.

text.description:
Megami Bridge is number 19 on the Nagasaki map, and it is a spot where the view of the structure matters more than any single detail on it. The phone icon on the map is about 320 m north-east of the subject. That makes it a good place for a wide, scene-setting photo for a travel album or a message home.

Use the gridlines on your phone and set the line of the bridge along one of the horizontal lines, so it does not appear to tilt. Leave some sky or water around it, as this gives a calm, uncluttered picture.

Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall view. If the bridge looks small, move to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter picture that also pulls the background closer. Tap on the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure control down a little if the sky is washing out. Take a few frames, since wind, passing traffic or boats can change the picture from one shot to the next.

We have no history, size or opening dates for this bridge, so the map keeps to the photo advice. Take care near any road or path, and keep clear of traffic while you frame your shot.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day with the sun behind you or to one side, so the bridge is lit rather than dark against the sky. Early morning or later in the day often gives softer light.
